Where does the pay raise go? Chart prices, lifestyle choices and future saving

Use four charts to separate take-home income growth, rising prices and lifestyle expansion, then follow the monthly surplus and the savings it can build.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore income growth, price changes and lifestyle expansion

Interactive planning lab

Saved-surplus portfolio at the selected finish date$211,094.21
Cumulative living costs without an income source$2,417.83
Portfolio in starting-price dollars$142,060.35

Hypothetical constant-rate planning exercise. Year 1 uses the entered monthly take-home income and expenses; annual increases first apply in year 2. Later expenses multiply both the price factor and the lifestyle factor, so their combined growth is (1 + price growth) × (1 + lifestyle expansion) − 1. Positive monthly surpluses are deposited at month-end; an equivalent monthly return compounds existing savings first. Negative surpluses are recorded as unfunded living costs, with no debt and no withdrawals from the saved-surplus portfolio. If that gap is positive, the displayed portfolio is conditional on finding other funding or reducing expenses. No opening investments, tax calculation, benefit changes, fees, irregular bills or salary forecast is included. Starting-price portfolio values deflate the finish-date balance over the full selected horizon; income and expense levels are constant within each year.

The central idea

A higher income creates room for a choice. The saving outcome depends on how living costs grow alongside it, and any spending above income still needs a funding source.

01

Begin with take-home income and actual living costs

The example begins with CAD 5,000 a month after payroll deductions and CAD 4,200 of monthly living expenses. That leaves CAD 800 available for saving. There is no starting portfolio in this comparison, so all later invested money comes from positive monthly surpluses.

The income growth input is an assumption about net pay. It cannot be read directly from a quoted gross salary increase: changes in tax, benefit deductions, pension contributions and working hours can change what reaches the account. Enter the amount available to spend after those effects have been considered separately.

Year 1 uses the starting amounts for all twelve months. The first annual increases arrive in year 2. This convention lets you read the first point directly against the opening budget. It also means a twenty-year illustration contains nineteen increases in the annual income and expense levels, while investments experience twenty years of monthly compounding.

02

Separate a higher price from consuming more

The model gives expenses two distinct drivers. Price growth changes the cost of the existing spending basket. Lifestyle expansion changes the quantity or quality consumed, such as adding trips, buying more services or choosing a more expensive version of a purchase. A larger family or a new care need can also increase consumption without representing a discretionary upgrade.

The two factors multiply. With 2% price growth and 2% lifestyle expansion, combined annual expense growth is 1.02 × 1.02 − 1 = 4.04%. Simply adding them gives an approximation, but misses the interaction. The first chart applies the full compounded relationship.

The comparison case sets lifestyle expansion to zero while retaining the same starting expenses and price increases. Its nominal bills still rise. It represents a constant modeled consumption basket, rather than a frozen dollar budget. Neither case predicts what your household will need or prefer over twenty years.

03

Read the difference between income and expenses

At the default settings, take-home income grows by 3% a year while expenses grow by 4.04%. The monthly surplus initially remains positive but gradually narrows. By year 20, monthly income is about CAD 8,767.53 and living costs are about CAD 8,913.65, leaving a CAD 146.12 monthly funding gap.

The surplus chart makes that crossing easier to see than two rising lines alone. A growing paycheque can coexist with less money available for goals. Conversely, if income grows faster than the existing-basket cost, holding lifestyle expansion lower can gradually increase the surplus without a one-time spending cut.

Actual expenses rarely follow smooth curves. A mortgage payoff, new housing arrangement, dependent or health expense can cause a step change. Use this chart to identify the question, then replace the smooth assumption with the relevant event when building a detailed household plan.

04

Follow deposits and keep unfunded spending visible

Each positive monthly surplus enters the portfolio at month-end. Existing investments first earn the equivalent monthly rate (1 + annual return)1/12 − 1. The 5% annual default is a hypothetical effective return, with no guarantee and no market volatility. The two cases earn the same rate, so different deposits drive their different balances.

The selected example accumulates about CAD 211,094 by the finish date. However, it also contains about CAD 2,418 of cumulative living costs without an identified income source. The model does not borrow or sell investments to pay that gap. Its displayed portfolio is therefore conditional on separately funding the shortfall or changing expenses. It is not a complete forecast of spendable household wealth.

The starting-price metric divides the finish-date portfolio by twenty years of the selected price-growth factor. It is about CAD 142,060 in the example. That conversion answers a purchasing-power question; it does not settle the cash shortfall, account tax treatment or investment risk. Read both the nominal balance and its conditions.

05

Decide where the next raise should go

The matrix reports final-year monthly income less final-year monthly expenses across different net-pay increases and lifestyle expansion rates. Negative cells are explicit funding gaps. Investment returns do not affect those cells because they measure the living budget before portfolio deposits or withdrawals.

  1. Update the budget using the actual change in net pay.
  2. Identify price increases and necessary changes in household needs.
  3. Choose the amount available for additional discretionary spending.
  4. Assign a sustainable saving transfer to specific goals.
  5. Review both the next-year budget and the later-year gap.

The FCAC’s budgeting guidance includes updating a budget after a pay raise or bill increase. The charts here make that review quantitative. They help locate a trade-off; they do not prescribe a universal spending-growth limit or a required savings rate.
